the-puri-teens: I know that many gen zers are having sex frequently and happily — I have overheard real Sex and the City-type brunches and walked into more than a few wonderfully graphic conversations in nightclub bathrooms — but when I think about my 10 closest friends, I can only think of two or three who have had sex or any type of sexual experience at all. There is no doubt that self-selection plays a role here — I’m fishing in the sexless ivory tower of academia, and I enjoy reserved people, so my friends are far more likely to be overly analytical and celibate than just any gen zer picked out of a crowd. However, while I also think of myself as more reserved, I have had a lot of enthusiastic, shame-free sex with multiple long-term partners, making me far from the imagined gen z “puri-teen.” I’ve dated a lot, explored all sorts of sexual subcultures, and logged heaps of softcore films on Letterboxd; I have also studied sex sociologically and philosophically at UChicago.

The puritanical ways of my beloved friends are baffling to me. What is throwing them into this arrested development? We grew up at the same time, have similarly privileged middle- or upper-class backgrounds, and consume the same media. Yet for each of my still-virginal friends, sex remains a far-away possibility.

Every analysis I read about why my generation is not having sex seems too broad, too sweeping; commonly cited external factors like “political anxiety” or “the lack of third spaces” do not explain my friends’ behavior — these reasons are structural, but sex is personal. Still, as much as I loathe the endless churn of gen z panic dreck, I morph into a millennial media monster when the topic of sex comes up. 1 “Have More Sex, Please!” I hear myself yelling in a clean, NYT Cheltenham font, over and over.

In lieu of an explicit, mimosa-laden brunch, I elected to interview a few of my friends and get to the bottom of their abstinence through another, perhaps more important question: when I ask them to have sex, what do I really want for them?
city-of-magnificent-intentions: Walking down Washington, D.C.’s empty streets, one gets the persistent feeling that the city is vanishing into thin air. In some sense, it is, because every two years, many of the city’s most important residents just pack up and go away. As a child of divorce, I sympathize with the city of Washington. It seems somehow right and proper to me that the seat of the United States government should be such a lonely, empty shithole.

I arrived in Washington in late May to study the Middle East at a well-respected think tank that I expected to resemble the lowest floors of my college library, where they keep the maps and encyclopedias. I was surprised to find the place crawling with young people. 25-year-old fellows oversaw 23-year-old program managers, who oversaw me and the other 21-year-old interns. Everyone flashed big smiles and waggled their eyebrows attentively when they were addressed by a superior.

It was often over 100 degrees outside the office building where I worked, and I lived very far from the office, which was itself very far down from Capitol Hill. The Hill is mysteriously bare of train, bus, or bike stations — it’s as if the congresspeople and their staffers are spirited to their assigned offices by transiting underground tunnels. And in fact they do exactly that. But as a newcomer from New York, I had no idea, and it was not until September that I learned about the tunnels.

In such heat, the only people out on the street are members of Washington’s formidable homeless population, dozing naked halfway out of the shade at bus stops, sheets of sweat washing over their swollen bellies and soaking into the sidewalk. One evening, a scary-looking dude ran after my bicycle, explaining that he was a veteran, that it was “Afghanistan all over again,” and that he was going to shoot me with a rifle. On another occasion, I witnessed an old, leathery man masturbate through his pants and then lie motionless on the grass.

A few months before I arrived in Washington, the situation became exaggerated when the city’s main sewer line burst and spewed forth nearly 300 million gallons of raw sewage, complicating the atmospheric chemistry within the miasmatic “heat domes.” So I would storm up the Hill every afternoon through a thick fog — thighs pumping madly, sweating through a thick suit — to show my respect to the congressional staffers by arriving on time for meetings to which they came late and about which they sometimes displayed some last-minute trepidation, wondering how Swamp Thing had made his way into a government building and whether he was really a member of their congressman’s district. Once, I was momentarily refreshed on my commute by a thin stream of water running down my forehead and onto my face from the trees above; I looked up just in time to see a squirrel shake the last droplets of piss from his tail before disappearing into the canopy.
depleted-shells: In Coumba Samba’s visual art, familiar objects and bright colors create a Lynchian experience of domesticity; malicious forces lurk beneath her shiny surfaces. With “Stars and Stripes,” Samba presents her first solo exhibition in the United States and becomes, at only 26, one of the Whitney Museum of American Art’s youngest-ever solo exhibitors. Her previous projects often feature found objects which encapsulate the global supply chain’s exploitation of African countries; the mundane in her installations straddles the gap between everyday existence and international politics, often amassing depth as unplumbable as the supply chain itself in doing so. Her primary pursuit as a visual artist is most effective when it simultaneously holds the intimate and international realms in perspective to highlight the individual’s role in complex systems of modernity. “Stars and Stripes” attempts a similar maneuver for the issue of nuclear development, but Samba loses sight of the very individuals she seeks to educate and implicate.

I enjoy considering each of Samba’s engagements with the arts — music, fashion, visual — as a part of a greater philosophy in “herself-as-readymade.” She moonlights as a singer in the cheekily-named electronic duo (and recent ear opener) New York and as a model for luxury fashion houses like Balenciaga. But while shooting editorials or making trendy glitchpop, she does not simply mannequin luxury clothing or set the language of the Internet to song; she embodies the strange encounters caused by globalization. Although she has lived and worked in Europe since her undergraduate studies, New York is the city of her birth and part-time residence, and her dual identity as both a Senegalese-American resident of the US and UK and an artist interested in history’s present manifestations exposes the economics which make possible that clothing’s and music’s existence.
coxon-day: It just so happened that the day everything changed, the day AI safety went mainstream, I was sitting in a multi-story fortress of autists and cracked researchers in Berkeley, California called Constellation, the center of what can only be termed The Resistance — a place that hums with excitement, and fervor, and a terrific sense that humanity is aboard a fast-moving, many-trillion-dollar locomotive called Artificial Intelligence, that the train is careening toward doom, and that this makeshift AI safety movement, brewing for decades in the dank parts of the internet and now headquartered in the East Bay, is the only thing that can stop it.

That day, September 8th, was the day Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old ML researcher, resigned from Anthropic, warning: “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Anthropic’s Alignment Science lead, Evan Hubinger, then quote-tweeted Coxon: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” By September 9th, Jacob’s tweet had made every front page and nightly news program in America. The ensuing maelstrom of discourse, in a matter of hours, brought “x-risk” and “p(doom)” from the fringes of American intellectual life to the bull’s-eye of public consciousness. Eliezer Yudkowsky, the portly forefather of the AI safety movement, declared momentary victory on X, the agora of AI: “Happy Coxon Day to all who will one day celebrate it.”

Over the next decade, our political life will undergo a total transformation. The tectonic continents of Left and Right will shudder, fracture, and re-form. Ideas and ideologies, so long fossilized in our institutions, will be liquidated and repoured. The first glimmers of that societal revolution are, right now, appearing all around us. But the battle lines of this new era will be drawn from geography altogether strange and foreign to the electorate: the once obscure, and often extreme, Bay Area factions that have so long labored and lamented over the most significant technological creation of our time.
mcnally-the-younger: It’s opening night at George McNally’s restaurant Faux. George is going around in a suit (a great suit, I might add) greeting the I-know-your-dads and I-invested-money-into-this-so-you-have-to-think-I’m-cool-and-maybe-they-ares? with bravado. He is, after all, the son of famous New York restaurateur and memoirist Keith McNally.
safe-at-slutcon: The two men in our circle were about what I expected. Both were readers of the blog LessWrong and worked for some kind of amorphous tech venture. The other girl and I were “flirt girls,” a compensated worker or volunteer whose job for the weekend was to let men practice flirting on them. The four of us sat cross-legged on a mattress somebody had pulled to the floor. The mattress was so soft that every time the girl next to me shifted her weight, I slid toward her. The people at Lighthaven call this practice “circling”; it asks you to narrate your inner state to others while it happens. If your throat dries when someone looks at you, you announce the dryness to the group.

I was dressed in my nondescript college girl outfit: a white top and jeans. The other girl wore black arm sleeves and eyelash extensions. When it was her turn to report, she said she felt bored. I’m good at flirting, and it isn’t hard to get a man to sleep with you, she said. Once I start, I can see exactly where the evening will end. Here, she told me that she felt like an “apex predator.” I laughed. Then I sat there sinking into the mattress, trying to work out what the laugh was for.

It was my first time at SlutCon, a three-day retreat in Berkeley for men who wanted to get better at seduction. It was my first time at Lighthaven, the venue that hosted it. I had never been to Lighthaven, but it reminded me of my co-op at Stanford. There was an open kitchen stocked with more food than anyone could eat. People were wealthy — I mean, “high-trust” — enough to leave their laptops lying around. The sunlight was Californian cashmere on the skin. We often sat on the ground like college kids. People were visibly nude or Dionysian in places, but the atmosphere as a whole still struck me as neutered and millennial, like a hackathon that had changed its prize.

Lighthaven used to be a hotel, and it still has a hotel’s bones — it has courtyards and garden paths. Now it is operated by Lightcone Infrastructure, an organization closely associated with a subculture known as “rationalism,” which formed online in the 2000s around writers including Eliezer Yudkowsky, Robin Hanson, and now Scott Alexander. The subculture is interested in avoiding cognitive biases and applying Bayesian inferences toward real-world objectives, including artificial intelligence alignment.
long-covid: There are a lot of people still masking. You tend not to notice them, since their faces are covered, but they are there, always anonymous and in the background: tearing your ticket at AMC, reading on the train, shopping at the grocery store. Oftentimes they walk with a cane. You see only their eyes; it’s like looking at half a person.

I’ve seen people like this around, masked students at school with strange hair and chunky boots. I’d register their existence with curiosity but nothing more, until I discovered Maddie Blair, the 25-year-old editor of Dublin- and Chicago-based literary magazine Sabr Tooth Tiger. She posts almost daily on Instagram, and since we had both been editors-in-chief — 4 years apart — of the same arts journal at the University of Illinois, I would come across one of her posts almost every day. Who was this doe-eyed, dark-haired girl, I wondered, and why was she still posting about Covid?

Maddie is what you might call Covid-cautious (alternatively “Covid-safe,” or “anti-disease”), and it was through her Instagram I stumbled upon a constellation of Chicago-based Discord chats, mutual aid organizations, community groups, dating events, advocacy networks, Instagram pages, and even one “black centered, burlesque and drag variety show” dedicated to spreading the good word about masking, which seems to come in a package with a whole bunch of other ostensibly leftist political priorities. In July, one such organization, Clean Air Club, which distributes air-purifiers and masks, advertised three “Covid-safer” events (air purifiers on site, masks required) hosted by various organizations across the city on their Instagram: a “Somatic Healing Dance (BIPOC-only event),” a “Joy Ryde Drag Show,” and a “Book Talk with Emmaia Gelman and Summer Institute: Why We Need to #DropTheADL from Schools.” Clean Air Club is the most legitimate of these Covid-conscious organizations, boasting a profile in The Guardian and a partnership with the Illinois Department of Public Health on another July Instagram post. It felt to me that serious and strange political energies had begun to coalesce around this issue of masking, and I wanted to find out how seriously they needed to be taken.
high-school-or-claude: This summer I heard various rumors coming out of Manifest (the prediction market conference held annually in Berkeley) that an unusually young kid named Eli Goldfine was wandering the Lighthaven grounds. The 14-year-old, I was told, had traveled there with his dad to interview Robin Hanson, the peculiar economist and prediction market forefather. Eli had also recently gotten into a fight with his middle school’s administration for betting on Manifold (the playmoney market that hosts Manifest) that he’d win co-chair in his class election (Eli won). And, most curiously, so the rumor went, Sam Bankman-Fried’s parents now wanted Eli to manage their jailed son’s Twitter account.

The 9th grader from Westchester, NY is part of the first wave of AI-conscious wunderkinds, self-starters without facial hair who, in the parlance of Silicon Valley, just build, learn, and do things. Eli hosts The Supercycle, a podcast on prediction markets, one of his many projects (e.g. coordinating underutilized, consumer-grade Seestar telescopes to perform follow-ups on certain objects that big, fancy, completely-booked telescopes can’t).

As Eli tells it, his edge is that, unlike his peers playing sports or video games, he cares about things that actually matter (philosophy, government, economics, astronomy, AI, prediction markets) — and not just for reasons of parental expectation or social status.

Eli is a precocious fellow, certainly, but he also represents the future of learning: self-education through AI. Eli started high school a few days after we spoke in August, much to his own chagrin. “If I had good AI ed tech, I could get through high school in a year or less,” Eli said on Liron Shapira’s podcast Doom Debates. “I don’t have any domain expertise in software engineering in the slightest.” He then described his workflow on various projects as “basically alternating between Claude, Codex, Twitter, and Substack all day...I’ve [just] never hit a wall where I need a human to go and do something.”
mrbeast-slop-auteur: Would you do what it takes for wealth and fame? Would you humiliate, debase, and torture yourself for a shot at stardom? There is a man who has done what it takes to become rich and famous, and he now tirelessly uses his wealth and fame to put other people in humiliating, debasing, and torturous situations for their own opportunities at success. Before that, though, he was a nobody with a dream. His dream was YouTube fame, and the only way he could achieve this dream was through understanding its algorithm.

Raised an evangelical by a single mother in Greenville, North Carolina, he was an introvert with consuming obsessions. As a youth, his obsessions were split between YouTube and baseball. He even hoped to become a MLB player. But this idea was crushed when he was diagnosed at the age of 15 with Crohn’s disease. The strain this condition put on his body forced him to give up on baseball and retreat indoors. He saw potential in online video creators who were starting to make real money in brand deals: YouTube would be his salvation.

He soon joined a group of other minor YouTubers who spent 10 hours a day studying how to go viral. He learned how to make the optimal title and thumbnail, along with hundreds of other minute aspects of editing, lighting, and pacing that gain and maintain attention. But despite his efforts, the algorithm was cruel. By the age of 19, after seven years of toil, he had been lucky enough to make a few dollars. He ceased to care about money, or art, or even love. He cared only about YouTube.

But after an entire youth wasted, after being unable to speak to kids at school about anything other than YouTube — and even then, his obsession for the topic often drove everyone away from discussing it with him — after dropping out of community college and being kicked out of his home by a mother who knew in her heart that her son was ruining his God-given life by spending it on a website dominated by children and gamers, the young man was finally about to become somebody. Grimacing, he sat in his chair, turned on the camera, and spoke.
jasmine-suns-project-of-self-transformat: Jasmine Sun is the author of the popular Substack “Jasmine’s Substack.” She is a contributing writer to The Atlantic, has published multiple pieces in The New York Times, and was recently interviewed by Ezra Klein. Her beat is the technologies and social mores of Silicon Valley. In her writing about Chinese peptides, the “permanent underclass,” and the furor over the construction of data centers, she has become the go-to “anthropologist of disruption.” She is 26.

“I’m only interested in people engaged in a project of self-transformation,” Susan Sontag wrote in her journals. Jasmine connected with that quote immediately upon reading it: she has been engaged in that project for a long-time. She joined the 826 writing seminars at 8-years-old, and was a champion high-school debater. At Stanford, she realized that the start-up world was a matter more of knowing the language than anything else, so she read the Silicon Valley canon. When she couldn’t get a job as a journalist, she started work at Substack, eventually becoming a project manager leading the core product team, before resigning to write full-time.

In her advice to college graduates of the class of 2026, Jasmine writes: “The old world was bad. Those staid institutions and rigid hierarchies are not worth mourning.” We can no longer expect that going to the right schools and checking the right boxes guarantees a life of wealth and flourishing; that world is gone. In this world where Substack, San Francisco, and AI all determine our future, we all have something to learn from Jasmine Sun.

I, unfortunately, did a lot of competitive debate growing up, so this is probably a big part of why I feel reasonably comfortable speaking on podcasts. I spent a lot of time doing the kind of debate in high school where you talk about critical theory at 300 words per minute. I feel like everybody in that community senses an affinity with others — I can name all of the other writers who used to be policy debaters off the top of my head. Ben Lerner did Policy, Sally Rooney did British Parliamentary, Nate Silver was a Policy debater, Jay Caspian Kang was a Policy debater, Kelsey Piper was a Policy debater, and Jerusalem Demsas debated, too.
the-striver-class: I’m worried nostalgia is a fascist emotion, I once announced to my law school housemate, a man who was forcefully subjected to my internal monologue for over two years. Gideon would consider my claim while reheating his leftovers. So is hunger, he’d rejoin, gesturing at the microwave. Then I would go upstairs and be nostalgic anyway.

I recently graduated from one of the top law schools in the United States. While I was there, I became terribly nostalgic for my childhood. It wasn’t because I had a good childhood. I grew up in a troubled household in New Zealand. Neither of my parents went to college; my grandparents are illiterate. We were constantly in debt, and everyone in my family blamed each other for it. Nothing about my upbringing involved unusual disadvantage, but I don’t think I met anyone else at my law school whose parents owed them money. People like Gideon were far more common there; his grandfather was an alum, and he had parents in academia. So my nostalgia puzzled me at first, because I was deeply unhappy in New Zealand. But after law school, I realized I missed reading the phrase “making the world a better place” without experiencing its mandatory sarcastic aftertaste. I missed not knowing how power really worked.

A selective law school is simultaneously serious and unserious. It’s a trade school, but it’s also a finishing school. In the United States, it is often a pipeline to the political class, so it has to be taken seriously as a culture; simultaneously, non-interdisciplinary legal academia is a joke, and law reviews may be the most embarrassing form of knowledge production on the planet. When you enter a selective law school, the world you come to reside in becomes extraordinarily parochial. I attended an elite institution as an undergraduate, too, but even a college with billionaires still has thousands of students majoring in diverse fields — the population is large enough to disappear into. Elite law schools permit no such disappearance. Mine had the class size of a high school and the claustrophobic social dynamics to match.
present-at-the-creation: Two years ago, the chief-of-staff to Anthropic’s CEO declared, “These next five years might be the last few years that I work.” At the time, she spoke for a world that knows far more about the future than the average American. But even before the release of ChatGPT, Theo Jaffee knew that the future was happening in the West. The 21-year-old University of Florida drop-out found his computer science classes in Gainesville pointless; they operated under old assumptions about how to build a career. Come summertime, he left for San Francisco, drawing on connections with former Curtis Yarvin intern Stevie Miller, attending the Manifest conference in Berkeley, and building out his Twitter following. Now Jaffee is the co-founder of Monitoring The Situation (MTS), an Andreesen-Horowitz backed media company that streams interviews of central players in AI and technology all day on X (formerly Twitter). Jaffee is San Francisco’s go-to reporter and AGI discussant, tirelessly cataloguing, describing, and perhaps influencing the future of our world.

A Spanish ruler declared long ago, “Had I been present at the Creation, I would have given some useful hints for the better ordering of the universe.” But if you cannot be present at the creation — well, at least you can monitor the situation. Below, I talk to Jaffee about becoming “AGI-pilled” and what we should do to prepare for a superintelligence we’re all underestimating.

This was my freshman year of college. I didn’t have an internship for that summer, so I decided — kind of like one of these people I knew from Twitter, Dwarkesh Patel — I would start a podcast where I’d find people I liked on Twitter and interview them. This was summer of 2023, three years ago now. I started interviewing a few people. My first guest was Greg Fodor. Some of the more famous people I interviewed were Zvi Mowshowitz, Robin Hanson, Bryan Caplan, and so on. I did maybe 20 episodes over the two years of the podcast — I definitely should have done more.

In August 2023, I visited SF for the first time. I didn’t meet any mutuals then, but I discovered the city and fell in love with the place. I was like, “Wow. It’s beautiful, it’s full of technology and tech people — I definitely need to be here after college.” I don’t love the city as much anymore, but I still love the people.
the-unstageable: Before the mid-19th century, reading a new book required a bit of preparation: you had to cut every single page loose with a knife. But to make Daniel Gavilovski’s three-play collection Carbon Pages, published by Unreal Press earlier this year, readable, you should simply take your knife and remove the full text of the first and third plays, as well as the preface. 1 Now, Gavilovski is a talented writer and a serious playwright — these plays have been staged, except for No Weapon Formed Against You, his “attempt at epic drama,” which has “eluded all attempts.” 2 But if you don’t take blade to page as I suggest, it is unlikely you will get far enough into Carbon Pages to realize this.
the-new-statesman: A rarely remarked-upon corollary to the supposed death of reading would be the death of literary style — the absence of young writers more famous for being in the world than for writing about it, who cultivate a look for the jacket cover, the camera, and the cocktail hour. But reading is not dead, nor is literary style. Need we look further than George Monaghan?

Monaghan is the newly appointed Newsletters Editor at Britain’s The New Statesman, where he was formerly Junior Commissioning Editor. For Monaghan, there need not be a trade-off between pleasure and writing; the 27-year-old talks about literature not with brooding melancholy, but with a grin. He evades the depressed, self-imposed asceticism of the lonely writer toiling away in obscurity, all while remaining serious about literature.
George and I discuss London’s contemporary intellectual life and the ambitions of young and optimistic British writers in an age of literary pessimism.
the-doctor-of-girlhood: Over the past few years, researchers and professors have put their heads down and uncovered a set of statistics about gen z ineptitude that we can all recite in our sleep now: we are more anxious, more lonely, and less likely to go out with friends or on dates; we’re having less fun and less sex, destroying our bodies, and melting our minds.
change-my-mind: The spectacle of online debate, of “owning the libs,” is now a rite of passage for the budding conservative commentator. Shabbos Kestenbaum, a 26-year-old Orthodox Jew, is the latest in this tradition of fast-talkers, a professional lineage that includes Charlie Kirk and Ben Shapiro. A quick Google search displays videos of Shabbos “debunking Anna [sic] Kasparian’s deranged conspiracies straight to her face,” and a photo of Shabbos and Sebastian Gorka (Trump official and dismantler of America’s counter-terrorism apparatus) smoking cigars on July 4th.

But before October 7th, Shabbos was a member of the Democratic Party, a Bernie Sanders supporter, and master’s student at Harvard Divinity School. A few months later, Shabbos had sued Harvard for antisemitism (in May of 2025, he agreed to a confidential settlement); his political star began to rise.

In 2024, Kestenbaum spoke at the Republican National Convention (“I am a proud first-generation American, I am a proud Orthodox Jew, and as of five months ago, I am the proud plaintiff suing Harvard University for its failure to combat antisemitism”) and endorsed President Trump; later, The New York Times profiled Kestenbaum as “The Jewish Student Who Took On Harvard.”

Now Shabbos works as commentator for PragerU, a publication and YouTube channel founded by Dennis Prager that “helps people of all ages think and live better while upholding Judeo-Christian values.” He lives in Los Angeles, where he makes podcasts and YouTube videos, and travels the country raising money for Zionist causes while warning of antisemitism’s corrosive spread.
What follows is Shabbos’s own articulation of his ideological journey.
manifest-man: On a cool June evening in Berkeley, I watched a man named Victor try to shoot a beam of light out of his penis. Minutes earlier, he had raised his hand because he found the volunteer onstage before him attractive. And now here he was, facing her in front of a crowd of perhaps 60 people, having been instructed to do precisely this by a woman named Aella, a pseudonymous camgirl and self-described sex researcher. She had promised the men in the room that the exercise, if undertaken in earnest, might actually result in hookups, real ones. Now she told her first subject to imagine himself gathering all of the energy in his body into his pelvis and then sending that energy outward as a beam of light, straight through his trousers and into the room.

Victor pointed out that this seemed a little absurd, which it manifestly was. But he did it anyway, standing there and trying — and you could see him trying — to imagine himself emitting light from the tip of his penis. Aella reported that Victor wasn’t shooting enough light, and he readjusted. She and the volunteer watched. The rest of us did, too. And then the volunteer delivered her verdict, which was that Victor had come up short. She had, in fact, “felt more” from him a moment earlier, before he’d begun to imagine light streaming out of his phallus.

This was Manifest, and Victor’s ordeal belonged to its official programming. The conference — this was its fourth iteration — convenes each summer at Lighthaven, a verdant complex of gardens and halls in a converted Berkeley hotel that rationalists keep as a gathering place. At Manifest, rationalism has little to do with Descartes; it’s a Bay Area subculture built around the site LessWrong, a “community blog” preoccupied with mathematics, philosophy, genetics, and the apocalyptic risks (and opportunities) presented by artificial intelligence.

Around 800 people attend Manifest each year. It takes its name, and its nominal subject, from Manifold, a prediction market. At the opening assembly, Austin Chen, co-founder of Manifold, asked everyone who had ever bet on it to stand, and very nearly the whole audience got to its feet. Officially, then, this is a conference about forecasting. But “a conference about prediction markets” describes Manifest about as well as “a conference about effigies” would describe Burning Man. Prediction markets are what the attendees have in common, but they are not, mostly, what they came to discuss.
behaving-badly: There seems to be about one movie a year that manages to penetrate the zeitgeist. This year, it appears to be Obsession. In a little over a month, on a budget of $750,000, it has grossed nearly $330 million. Instagram, X, and TikTok are flooded with stills, clips, frame-by-frame analyses, deep-dive video essays, cultural commentaries, and AI-generated tweets about the movie. Like Backrooms director Kane Parsons, 26-year-old Obsession writer-director Curry Barker got his start on YouTube, releasing horror short The Chair in 2023 and feature Milk and Cereal in 2024 before signing a deal with Focus Features, a real distributor, and bringing Obsession into the world two years later. He’s been tapped as the next director of the Texas Chainsaw Massacre franchise, and in June, he signed an 8-figure deal to direct a horror film with Universal.
the-commodification-of-freya-india: Maybe you have heard of Freya India. She is a frequent guest on podcasts hosted by middle-aged men, her interviews are clipped into Reels and TikToks and reposted all over the internet, and she has over 54,000 subscribers on Substack.

India paints a dystopian, conservative picture of the gen z woman, psychologically damaged by social media, porn, godlessness, decadence, and divorce. India, investigating the source of her own problems, applies her critique to the culture at large. Girls in general, she contends, feel like India once did — lonely, insecure, and scared.

India, hailing from Essex, England, is only 26. She’s a contributing writer at The Free Press and a contributing “Gen Z voice” for Jonathan Haidt’s After Babel. Now she’s written a mass-market book aptly titled Girls: The Commodification of Everything.
Fellow mass cultural critics have been quick to anoint her.
luddite-club: I am midway down South Street, phone in hand and footsteps fast. Every time I walk down this strip of sidewalk, I think of the time during freshman year when my friends peed somewhere along this street — wherever there was some small shred of privacy to be had — their Halloween costumes not nearly warm enough in the nippy fall air.

I am walking with my phone held in front of me, eyes on the solid blue line leading the way, looking up from Apple Maps to catch the snow, the frost dusting the concrete, remembering that Penn Museum is here, I think, noticing that there is some sun out, and it is illuminating a vaguely collegiate building past the intersection. I follow my phone like it is a shepherd. I remind myself that I am going somewhere new. As I cross S 33rd St, I pass itinerant figures heading in the same direction, some bunching at the intersection as I walk past, others speaking on the phone, someone loudly saying something about changing her mind.

I am cold but not that cold. I am too-aware of the block of earth metals in my hand that is receiving the brunt of my attention — only because I am following its directions, but still, it is ironic. I am slightly nervous because I have only ever seen the person that I am meeting in a picture from a New York Times article. I am walking into a coffee shop. I am meeting Biruk Watling, one of the original members of the New York Luddite Club (NYLC).

My mother scrolls Facebook in the passenger seat of the car, on the couch, in bed. I judge her for it, and then I open YouTube Shorts. Recently, she instated a new rule, one we never had as kids: phones in the kitchen by midnight. Last month, as I was plugging in my phone in the kitchen, I told my brother I wished the rule was for 11 o’clock rather than midnight. He said I could put my phone away then, no one’s stopping me. I said, “I know.”

We all talk about being addicted to our phones, but as far as I’ve heard, “addiction” is a term used casually, lightly, self-deprecatingly — like it’s simply an everyday practice that practically cannot be helped. It feels this way (bad, but not bad enough to feel agony over) partly because it seems like everyone does it. If phone and social media use is an addiction, one that prompts occasional invocations from our parents to give it up, these urges have felt more and more hollow of late.
